The purpose of the Bill is to establish for the next federal election electoral boundaries. Generally speaking, the Bill
wants to restructure the electoral boundaries map of Canada so that some provinces would get additional seats. Indeed, the Province of Ontario will end up with four more seats, the Province of British Columbia will end up with two more seats, and the remaining provinces will have the same number of seats as they presently have. My amendment does not interfere with the 99 seats which have been allotted to Ontario in the legislation. It indicates that that part of Ontario that is known as northern Ontario geographically and in common practice would maintain the 11 seats which that part of Ontario presently holds. We do not seek to add a greater number of seats to the Province of Ontario. We do not seek to reduce the number of seats in any other province. My amendment simply indicates that the 11 ridings in northern Ontario will be maintained.
I would suggest that this amendment falls well within the purpose and intent of the Bill. The intent of the Bill is to establish ridings which would return Members to the House of Commons at the next federal election. My amendment does not go beyond that principle. The principle of my amendment deals with the situation as it exists in the Province of Ontario. I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that my amendment is therefore in order.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join the debate with regard to the procedural acceptability of Motion No. 4. This morning the Chair indicated that it would like to hear arguments with regard to Motions Nos. 4 and 5. It seems to me that Motion No. 4 put by the Hon. Member is very similar to my Motion No. 5 except that Motion No. 5 sets out the exact geographic locations involved in northern Ontario and the 11 seats that exist there. As well, it sets out the procedure for redistributing those seats within the geographical area of northern Ontario.
I would argue that these motions are in order. Motion No. 4 simply seeks to amend one clause of Bill C-74. It essentially applies the same principle to a large geographic area in northern Ontario which represents 80 per cent of the land mass of the Province of Ontario as is applied to Saskatchewan and other provinces which are provided with a floor for representation under Rule 2 of which we have just approved.
The principle of Motion No. 5 is essentially the same one that was adopted by the Electoral Boundaries Commission which identified northern Ontario as a geographical location and accepted the present number of Members. The Commission adopted a population average of 70,000 for the area as opposed to the 81,000 which has been adopted for the rest of the province. The amendment simply applies to redistribution within the Province of Ontario and does not infringe upon any redistribution taking place in other provinces. 1 would argue that Motions Nos. 4 and 5 are procedurally acceptable.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my actions with respect to this Bill have demonstrated the fact that I am prepared to listen to reason-
November 26, 1985

able suggestions for amendments. The motions I have put before the House at report stage reflect that.
I have listened with great interest to the representations made vis-a-vis the attempt to bring forward amendments at this stage of the Bill. I think the Bill already addresses the concerns that have been expressed in the amendments brought forward by Hon. Members. However, that is not why I am rising now.
I do not think that there is any question that these amendments are clearly out of order according to the rulings in Beauchesne's. Let me express why this is the case. In the first place, the amendment put by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) must be rejected because its wording is too vague. The Hon. Member refers to an area described as northern Ontario. Depending on whether one lives in Barrie, North Toronto or London, one's perspective of northern Ontario may include quite a variety of places and descriptions. The vague description of northern Ontario is not a clearly defined geographical area. Therefore-
Wait till I send this out to those Tory ridings.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am speaking in technical terms. We all know that northern Ontario is an important part of the country. However, the fact is that it is not a legally defined geographic entity in any official atlas and therefore is incapable of definition.
The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) identified certain areas in northern Ontario which would be entitled to a certain number of seats. However, both amendments, as Your Honour pointed out at the beginning of debate on report stage, are out of order since they depart entirely from the principle set down in this legislation.
Let me simply remind Your Honour of the fact that the principle of this Bill and the Act which is being amended by this legislation was not that we in Parliament define the location or number of seats within any province. Rather, that responsibility has been delegated to electoral commissions. These two amendments purport to take away that responsibility which is delegated under Section 13 of the parent Act, an Act which is not before the House. That is the principle under which the legislation operates. There are delegations of authority to the Electoral Commissions in each province.
In this case, the amendments purport or attempt to create different rules for the Province of Ontario than those that exist for any other province. The changes proposed to this legislation create one set of rules for all provinces across the country. There is delegation of responsibility within each province to the electoral commissions. However, these amendments would significantly depart from that principle by designating certain things for northern Ontario or for electoral districts in northern Ontario.
If accepted by Your Honour, these amendments would be contrary to the purpose of this Bill which provides rules to apply generally to all provinces. Therefore, on the face of it,
Representation Act, 1985
notwithstanding the merits of the case, they clearly depart from the principles of the Bill before us today.
You will of course, Mr. Speaker, be aware of Citation 773.(1) of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition which indicates that an amendment is out of order if it is irrelevant to the Bill, beyond its scope or governed by or dependent upon amendments already negatived. In conclusion, quite apart from the fact that we have dealt with the principles and objections that are contained within these suggested amendments, these amendments are clearly outside the scope of the legislation and contrary to the principles of the legislation. I would have to argue strongly with you, Mr. Speaker, that they are not in order. Having said that, however, there is no problem because the amendments I have brought forward are, in fact, dealt with and there will be equity for northern Ontario.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
After hearing the procedural arguments of the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) as to the acceptability of Motion No. 4, and even though there is some doubt in the mind of the Chair as to its procedural acceptability, it is the Chair's position that the doubt should be to the benefit of the Hon. Member. The same remarks apply to Motion No. 5 put forward by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster).
Having said that, the motions will be allowed to go forward, although I must indicate to the House that they will be debated together and voted on separately. Therefore, I will put the motions to the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Rodriguez (Nickel Belt) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 4
That Bill C-74, be amended in Clause 2 by striking out line 34 at page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
"of one, one other member.
4. Among the number of members assigned to Ontario, there shall be assigned a minimum of eleven members to Northern Ontario."

November 26, 1985
Representation Act, 1985

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate you on the fine, impartial wisdom of your ruling. There is a reason for moving the amendment which calls for a guarantee that the 11 seats in northern Ontario remain when the electoral boundaries map is drawn for the Province of Ontario.
Geographically, northern Ontario is a huge land mass with very little population. As a matter of fact the population has been declining. The experience in the past has been that when electoral boundaries maps are drawn and the hearings are held the commissioners are dealing with numbers. They have a floor and a ceiling. They have to create ridings between that floor and that ceiling to match the population of northern Ontario. As a result, we could have communities which are up to 800 to 900 miles apart falling within the same riding. The last time the electoral boundaries committee met to look at the electoral boundaries in Ontario there was a proposal with respect to the boundaries of the riding of Timiskaming coming into the riding of Nickel Belt and removing the community of Nickel Centre out of Nickel Belt and connecting it up to Timiskaming. This is a situation in which there was no historical or cultural relationship. There are great distances between the communities in the southern part of the riding compared with the northern part of the riding.
Not only would it be difficult for a Member of Parliament to serve such a riding, it would be difficult for his or her constituents to communicate effectively with the Member of Parliament. Indeed, I could get on to my bias and my horse and ride it. The fact is that the population in northern Ontario is declining. The decline closely parallels the decline in the resource sector. In fact, we have consistently argued that instead of reducing the number of voices in the legislatures, both provincial and federal, we should have more voices to balance the geographic and regional disparities which exist in that part of the province.
I am absolutely positive that if the commissioners were to look at the census figures at the present moment they would see that northern Ontario would suffer a loss of seats. 1 am absolutely sure of that. In fact, to do that would force the commissioners to look at wiping out a riding and bringing in groups from greater and greater distances to make up the nine or ten seats. I do not think that is fair to northern Ontario. The arguments end up like a dog trying to catch its tail. People say that if we can get more people to live in northern Ontario then we could have more seats. We have also heard that if we had more people living in the North we would have more industry. We know that is simply the old chicken and egg argument. It does not cut ice with us because we have experienced this. It seems to me we cannot apply a straight "rep by pop" application to northern Ontario. We have to look at the situation in terms of serving the people. That is what we have to look at- the quality of the service to the people. In fact, we have made these exceptions in the past.
I see the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) moving his head from right to left. We have made these types of exceptions. If one were to look at it one would see that Canada
is a study in exceptions. If representation by population were considered for Prince Edward Island then it ought not to have the number of seats which it now has. That includes all of the Atlantic region. However, because the Fathers of Confederation recognized that there were these anomalies in the country, and therefore the need to recognize those differences and to make sure the representation in the House reflected that, we do have a type of guarantee for parts of the country such as Prince Edward Island and other parts of Atlantic Canada. That is fair.
I argue in favour of the amendment which is before the House. It is only fair to the people of northern Ontario who are taxpayers and who deserve the same quality of service which a constituent living in downtown Toronto, the Beaches or some other southern riding deserves. It would not be a weakening of the electoral boundaries to guarantee northern Ontario its 11 seats. It seems to me it is a guarantee of participation in the democratic process.
I recommend the amendment to Members of the House. I am sure the Conservative Members who represent three ridings in northern Ontario would argue for the support of this amendment if they were here. I believe the three ridings are Timiskaming, Timmins-Chapleau and Nipissing. I ask these Members to try to impose this mesasure upon the Conservative Government. However, I am sure that when it comes time to vote they will want to vote it down. I wish to send this message out to all corners of northern Ontario. I want them to know that the Conservative Government is not prepared to give them a fair voice in this House. Those Hon. Members would be prepared to vote the amendments down.
Oh, oh!

Well, the vote will come and we will see how you are going to vote. We are going to send back a copy of Hansard on that day to folks living in those ridings you presently hold so they will be able to see how fair the Tories are. I ask Hon. Members opposite, I appeal to their sense of fair play, to support this amendment. If they do not, then they will vote against it to their everlasting sorrow.
Oh, oh!
Those Hon. Members laugh. They think it is funny.
Even your own people think it is funny.

There are cases where a person who lives 300 miles away from his Member of Parliament, has a problem, and wants to see his Member of Parliament. The Member of Parliament is very busy but that person wants to have access to him. That is when the application will strike home. That is when the practical application of the Tories' denial of northern Ontario maintaining its 11 seats will strike home. The proof will be in the eating of this pudding.

I call upon Hon. Members of the Conservative Party not to be stampeded by their House Leader. I urge them to stand up for northern Ontario. Give us the guarantee of 11 seats. It doesn't take anything away from them but it allows the people of northern Ontario to have fair representation in the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I believe your ruling was excellent. It was fair and well reasoned. It was an important decision for the Chair in this House of Commons with regard to Bill C-74, the Electoral Boundaries Redistribution Bill. I think it is absolutely essential that these amendments which were put forward with respect to northern Ontario are accepted by the House of Commons because this Bill is really designed to restrict the growth of the House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

It will in effect reduce the numbers of Members who will be provided to Ontario by six. It is interesting to hear Members opposite from the western provinces arguing for reduced representation. If the Hon. Member opposite who just spoke from his seat had really argued for the benefit of Alberta, he would have stated as soon as this Bill was introduced that it was unfair to Alberta because it reduced the representation to which Alberta was entitled.
So what?

The Hon. Member says: "So what?" Does he not want to see Alberta have its proper representation? I certainly want to see northern Ontario have its proper representation because northern Ontario is a distinct geographical unit of some 88 per cent of the land mass of the province of Ontario. My constituency, which is of medium size by many standards, still encompasses 13,000 square miles and is over 500 miles long. Other constituencies such as Cochrane Superior, Kenora-Rainy River and Timiskaming are even larger. Those areas of Ontario want and deserve adequate representation in the form of at least 11 Members of Parliament.
I hope that Members opposite from northern Ontario-the Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall), the Hon. Member for Timmins-Chapleau (Mr. Gervais), the Hon. Member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Kelleher) and the Hon. Member for Nipissing (Mr. Mantha)-will come forward and lend their support. We are not doing anything in these amendments to take away from representation in other provinces. We are just saying that out of the 99 Members of Parliament, in the allocation of Ontario there should be at least 11 seats, one ninth, from northern Ontario. We have 88 per cent of the land mass but our population is not nearly as dense as it is, for example in Toronto.
These amendments provide that there will be at least 11 Members of Parliament to be a strong voice from the north in the Parliament of Canada. I think there is a precedent for this in the Ontario legislature brought in by the previous Conserva-
Representation Act, 1985
tive Government. The Hon. Member for Saskatoon, who is the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Hnatyshyn), is a great admirer and adherent of that former Tory Government. It provided 16 seats in the provincial legislature out of 124 or 125 Members. Surely, that precedent is a good one to follow in the Parliament of Canada. We are a distinct geographical area within the province of Ontario and these amendments do not in any way infringe on the electoral arrangements in other provinces. They simply ask for an adequate representation in the Parliament of Canada for northern Ontario within the Ontario allocation.
I think as time goes on, Mr. Speaker, this will be proved to be very wise because constituents demand more services from Members. They want to see their Members of Parliament at community functions. They want to be able to deal on a personal level with Members of Parliament. A reduction in the number of Members from northern Ontario would make this task, which is already difficult, almost impossible.
If we examine the Bill as it was put forward by the President of the Privy Council, we see that the population rises from some 81,000 as proposed in the existing amalgam program to 87,000. This new average population in Ontario will keep rising with each redistribution in the future and it is obvious that the Bill before the House today, Bill C-74, will reduce by six Members the representation as proposed in the existing redistribution legislation. It is impossible to believe that at least one or two Members either in this redistribution or in the next will not be lost from northern Ontario.
I submit that one Member of Parliament can easily look after 80,000 or 90,000 people in Metropolitan Toronto where there are constituencies of a couple of square miles as opposed to the ridings in northern Ontario which have as a minimum, something like 13,000 square miles, as in the case of Algoma. I certainly hope that Hon. Members opposite, including the President of the Privy Council who is a gentleman, scholar and a great Parliamentarian, will see the fairness of this amendment because he grasped the principle and applied it to his own province of Saskatchewan. He said: "We want to have a floor under the representation from the province of Saskatchewan", and he has provided that floor with Rule No. 2 and it provides for 14 Members of Parliament from the province of Saskatchewan with a population of 968,000. This amendment does not demand the kind of fairness which our side is prepared to provide to Saskatchewan.
Because the population of northern Ontario is something around 800,000, we would certainly be entitled to more than 11 seats, perhaps, but we are asking the President of the Privy Council to provide the same fairness for northern Ontario as he has provided for the province of Saskatchewan and his own constituency. There again, you are dealing with very large spaces but not nearly as large a constituency as we see in northern Ontario. Yet this Bill provides a grandfather clause which in effect adds three seats to the number Saskatchewan would otherwise be eligible for. The same thing applies in Manitoba where the population is almost exactly one million people. That works out to 11.7 Members. The Bill provides a

November 26, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
floor by adding two more so that Manitoba gets 14 Members even though it has only about 200,000 more people than northern Ontario.
In the interest of fairness, not just for the western provinces as provided by the grandfather clause, I hope the Minister will want to apply the same principle to northern Ontario. He can come to northern Ontario and talk to the people in Sault Ste. Marie, the constituency of the Minister for International. Trade He can talk to the constituents of the Hon. Member for Timmins-Chapleau, the Hon. Member for Timiskaming and the Hon. Member for Nipissing. Ask them whether or not there should be a floor. I am sure the Minister would be persuaded that these amendments set out a fair and equitable and just regime for an important area of our country. Northern Ontario has provided great Members of Parliament in the past. It has sent us a former Prime Minister, Lester Pearson, as well as great Speakers and cabinet Ministers. Last but not least it has also provided great private Members like those here who support this resolution this afternoon. I hope we have persuaded the Minister to give leadership to the private Members on his side so that he will lend his support to at least Motion No. 5 and perhaps Motion No. 4 as well. I hope we have persuaded the Minister to see the fairness of this amendment just as he saw its principle applied to his home province of Saskatchewan in the Bill now before the House.

Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by commending the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) for introducing Motion No. 5. In principle Bill C-74 has a great deal to commend it. I particularly want to congratulate the Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn) for improving the methodology of drawing constituency boundaries and giving the commissions much more latitude to take into account a community of interests and geographic size. Nevertheless, a special case can be made for the northern part of the Province of Ontario.
Or anybody.
No. That is where you are wrong. There is the voice of Toronto.
Oh, oh!
He is from Alberta.

I want to tell the Government House Leader that that is exactly the problem we have had in northern Ontario. The Toronto attitude is northern Ontario is nothing but the poor backyard, the hinterland of the province. They go in and grab the resources, take them somewhere else, move the money back and forth from hand to hand, institution to institution, and that is it. That is why we are making a plea for northern Ontario as a special case. It is not true that every province has a northern part which is precisely the same as Ontario. First of all, Ontario is one of the biggest provinces. Most of the province is in the North. For a long time northern
Ontario has had special status in many respects. If anyone here happens to follow a national sport called curling, they will know that each province enters its own team in national competition called the Briar. Northern Ontario has always had its own curling team in the Briar and, more often than not, and my colleagues from the North can correct me, we have taken the Briar. Because it is the dominant part of the province, northern Ontario requires special protection under the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act so that eventually we are not left with only three or four seats under redistribution.
We in northern Ontario have come to see the importance of federalism. On many occasions, when the voice of the North could not be heard in Toronto, we knew it could always be heard in this House. That is why you will find the strongest proponents of a strong federal system residing in northern Ontario. Let me go one step further and remind the House that what the Hon. Member for Algoma has done today is not some innovation which has never been heard of before. You will recall the election of 1979, if you want to call it that. It was kind of an abortive election because we were back at the polls again in 1980. However, that election was fought with new boundaries. Prior to that time, when the redistribution process had been completed, it was discovered that northern Ontario was going to lose part of its representation. One of the very large constituencies at that time was called Thunder Bay. That is not to be confused, I say to the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp), with the riding he now represents. It was at that time an entirely rural constituency. No part of the city was included. It was one of the largest constituencies in the country. As a result of redistribution, that constituency was done away with entirely. The House was quick to observe that a very grave injustice had been done to that great region of the country. In its wisdom the House sought to redress that grievance. One of the outstanding Government Members at that time, the late R. K. Andras, sensed the mood of the House. He knew this was the place where these injustices had to be corrected. Although the parliamentary timetable was completely filled up in the time leading up to the end of that session, he used political judgment and influence to convince the House Leader of the time to squeeze out a bit of time in which to redress this grievance of the people of northern Ontario. A Government Bill was introduced which was very similar in scope to the motion introduced today by the Hon. Member for Algoma. It was to give northern Ontario a floor representation. It did not ask for anything unreasonable, only to retain the level of representation which they had at that time.
The people of the north, in so many ways, regard themselves as being like a province. It is true that it is a region, but anyone who knows the spirit of northern Ontario knows that the people feel very much as though they are a province. In fact, there have been very vigorous movements in northern Ontario to actually create a Province of Northern Ontario. The name "Aurora" was once suggested. There was once a political party formed led by Mr. Ed Deibel from the commu-
November 26, 1985

nity of North Bay who proposed that there be a province formed, not separate from Confederation, but separate from the grasping hands of Toronto which wanted to take all of our riches and give us the dregs after they were through consuming the resources of the north.
There is a sense that we are a province. At that time we were asking for the same deal which the Province of Saskatchewan has in that it is guaranteed a floor. Although Saskatchewan is a full-fledged province in Confederation, we thought it was reasonable that we have the same thing. The late Hon. R. K. Andras, an outstanding Member of Parliament from Port Arthur, whose political leadership we miss, strengthened the political process in northern Ontario. He was so successful that at one time the Liberals held every seat across the north. That shows the kind of influence that that man had in northern Ontario and in the national life of the country.
It will be like that after the next election, too.

He introduced a Government Bill into the House. As I explained before, he had only a limited amount of time because the timetable was so full. We debated the Bill that afternoon and almost got it passed. It only required unanimous consent. Although the Members from Toronto were reluctant to agree, even they went along. Finally, only one lone Member, whose name and place of origin I will not mention, withheld consent. He is no longer here because he lost his seat in the infamous election of 1979. It could not have happened to a nicer guy. Because he withheld consent, the Bill did not pass and northern Ontario had to face a very serious disruption in the way in which it was represented in the House of Commons.
The Member for Algoma now wants to redress that grievance. He wants to correct something which should have been corrected in 1978. It failed only by the voice of one single Member, now departed from these august chambers. However, we are going to correct the injustice now. I am sure that Members opposite will help us. They will see that this is right. I know that the Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn) cannot help but support this. I want to commend, once more, the Member for Algoma for giving this kind of leadership to the rest of us in northern Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, as you are aware, I intervened in debate this morning. I want to tell you how pleased many of us on this side of the House were with the way in which you rendered your decision to allow both of these amendments to stand. I indicated this morning the importance of these amendments to northern Ontario. I also indicated why we in northern Ontario feel very strongly about the need for maintaining the present number of seats in order that we can do the work for our constituents in northern Ontario.
To digress somewhat from the remarks of the previous speaker, there are certain issues in our lives which transcend political philosophies and political parties. Frankly, I believe that this is one of those occasions. I would like to salute not
Representation Act, 1985
only the Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), but also the Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) who put forward an amendment to ensure that the representatives of constituencies in northern Ontario, regardless of which political Party they represent, will be able to represent the people of northern Ontario. The degree of representation in northern Ontario is very important to all residents there. The test of the Conservative Government will be the decision made by the representatives of the Conservative Party who represent the constituencies of Sault Ste. Marie, Timmins-Chapleau and Timiskaming. We on this side of the House want to see whether they will represent the interests of their constituencies by voting with us, rather than with the Government, to ensure that the number of constituency bases remains the same in northern Ontario.
The Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) has been very eloquent this afternoon in his praise of previous Members of Parliament who represented constituencies in northern Ontario. He mentioned the late R. K. Andras who represented the riding of Thunder Bay. As well, the late C. D. Howe represented that area of northwestern Ontario for years in the House of Commons. We have had a history of very strong representatives from northern Ontario. It would be a mistake for the House of Commons to eliminate a seat in northern Ontario simply through the pursuit of representation by population.
As I indicated this morning, Mr. Speaker, I am fortunate in that I represent the only urban riding in northern Ontario. My job is easier in terms of the amount of travel that I have to do. I can represent my constituency of Sudbury by simply flying into one urban centre. Of the 11 constituencies in northern Ontario, I am the only one to be so fortunate. The other 10 Members of Parliament from northern Ontario have to travel through connecting airports to finally reach the geographic centre of their constituencies. From that point they have to travel by car, float plane, or train in order to service the interests of their constituents.
Whether we accept the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt or that put forward by the Hon. Member for Algoma, it matters little. The important factor is that we retain the same number of constituencies in northern Ontario. I am sure that I speak for all of my colleagues on this side of the House when I say that we would welcome an intervention by the Conservative Members of Parliament who represent the constituencies of Sault Ste. Marie, Timmins-Chapleau, and Timiskaming. We would like them to stand up this afternoon and defend the interests of the constituents of northern Ontario. I hope that they will find it within the realm of possibility to vote against the Government's proposal. You know as well as I, Mr. Speaker, that in the quest for reform of the House of Commons it is very important to allow individual Members of Parliament to have a free vote. They should not be pressured by the Government or the Government House Leader. I am sure that he is not going to put the twist on their elbows, Mr. Speaker. Surely he would not do that.
There is only one Minister in the Government who represents the interests of northern Ontario, that is the Minister of

November 26, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
international Trade (Mr. Kelleher). The Minister, who represents the constituency of Sault Ste. Marie, has not been in the House to defend the interests of the constituents of northern Ontario.
Shame.
I think it is encumbent upon-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I must call the Member to order and remind all Members of the House that it is not permitted to remark on the presence or absence of other Members within the Chamber.
I will accept that ruling from you, Mr. Speaker. But, my heavens, I think it is rather telling that that Member would be missing on an important afternoon-
Order.

-when we are debating the future of the northern Ontario constituency base. I will accept your ruling and simply indicate that this is a typical case which we have witnessed time after time. The Government back-benchers who are elected by their constituents to represent their interests have been amazingly silent. Why should we from northern Ontario express any more surprise this afternoon? The backbenchers in the Conservative Party have been silent on issues of family allowance and the deindexation of senior citizen pensions. While a Minister of the Crown or a Parliamentary Secretary from the Government may not support these amendments, surely one could hope that the two other individuals who are not in Cabinet or Parliamentary Secretaries could indicate on the floor of the House this afternoon their support for the two amendments put forward by the Member for Nickel Belt and the Member for Algoma so that we could prevent this kind of disembowelling, if I may say so, of the interests of the constituents of northern Ontario.
I am sure that once I sit down, other Members on this side of the House will indicate their support for these two amendments. However, it will come as no surprise to me that once again there will be the typical silence from Government back-benchers.

Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to have this opportunity to join in the debate on this important matter. I want to recognize the insight and wisdom of the Speaker in ruling that the motions put forward by the Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) and the Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) are in order. I want to recognize in particular the foresight of my colleague, the Member for Nickel Belt, who is the dean of the northern Ontario caucus of the NDP, in putting this motion forward. Let me also recognize the support for regional realities in our province and country as displayed by the Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) when he seconded the motion of my colleague from Nickel Belt.
Other Members have addressed the importance of recognizing the extent of the geography of northern Ontario and having it properly recognized and represented in the House of Commons. This was referred to eloquently by the Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) in particular, who suffered cruelly in the redistribution of 1977. Of course, I might be of two minds about his praise for the Hon. Robert Andras, my worthy predecessor in what is now Thunder Bay-Nipigon. I am grateful that he was not running in the 1984 election, or things might have turned out somewhat different. Nonetheless, I want to recognize the efforts that have been made in maintaining representation for northern Ontario.
It was stated this morning that the part of the province north of the French River constitutes almost 88 per cent of the province. To have such a great geographic mass represented by only one-ninth of the Members of Parliament surely is a mean enough position to be in. I believe that our motion to maintain 11 Members in future Parliaments is surely appropriate to the geographic extent.
With respect to the sports history referred to by the Member for Cochrane-Superior, relating to the province of northern Ontario as recognized by the curlers of this country, I might note that it was not always that way. I believe it was approximately 1947 when the curlers in the City of Port Arthur and Fort William at the time and Sudbury looked at the situation carefully. The Sudbury curlers recognized the travel barriers they faced in going to Toronto to take part in provincial matches.
While that may have been manageable, the Lakehead curlers faced a different challenge. They were often in the Manitoba Briar playdowns and running into difficulties taking part in the semifinals in the City of Winnipeg. As the Hon. Member observed, they were fine curlers from northern Ontario and often represented Manitoba in the national Briar. Therefore, it proved to be desirable in these circumstances to create the province of northern Ontario and allow the curlers from that area of the province to compete in their own provincial play-down to send a team to the Briar. As the Hon. Member stated, we have done very well. We are certainly proud of A1 Hackner and his succession of rinks. speakeroldname: Mr. J. R. Ellis (Prince Edward-Hastings) moved
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-252, an Act to amend the House of Commons Act (estimates), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to thank my colleagues who will speak on the Bill as well this evening. As we all know, the hour provided for the consideration of Private Members' Business is now over an hour late. I appreciate those Hon. Members taking the time to stay and support the particular Bill. Also, at the outset, I want to say that Bill C-252 concerns the position of the Administrator of the House, not especially the person of the Administrator of the House.
The purpose of my Bill is very simple. It is outlined in the opening pages of the Bill under "explanatory notes". The purpose is to add the Administrator to those officers of the House of Commons who are responsible for preparing the estimates of the sums required for the House. The administration of the House of Commons has evolved from its inception in 1867. However, there are in fact a number of the 1867 rules still in effect. There were very few changes and no studies to speak of until 1964. The study which took place that year made, among others, three statements worth repeating. The first was:
The Clerk has had to spend a disproportionately large amount of his time in dealing with administrative and personnel matters.
The second was:
The study brought to light some 170 specific problems in the administration of the House of Commons.
Finally, and I quote again:
What is clearly needed is a revised structure which includes positions for administrators who have the time, the skill, and the authority to deal effectively with administrative and personnel problems.
For reasons which are slightly obscure now, this last recommendation was never carried out.
In 1975, a report entitled: The State of Administration in the Canadian House of Commons had the following to say:
If we look at the changes which have taken place in the administration of the House of Commons since 1867, we see that very few major changes have been introduced.
Let me now read a few quotes from the report of the Auditor General undertaken in 1979 and reported in 1980. Speaking of the heavy responsibilities of the then Clerk, Mr. Alistair Fraser, the report said that he had to spend "a disproportionately large amount of time on administrative and personnel matters". The report went on to outline, as a major deficiency, "the lack of a clear separation between the mainstreams of activities in the House-procedural duties and administrative responsibilities-resulting in the absence of
House of Commons Act
clearly defined administrative mandates, organizational relationships and delegations of authority". The last quote from the same report, where the Auditor General's major recommendation to solve one of the fundamental problems identified in 1964 but left unresolved, was to "establish the position of Administrator to co-ordinate and direct the administrative functions of the House of Commons".
Although 1 will be quoting further from these and other reports to support my Bill, I want to ask Members in the House to hark back to the statements attributed to the former Speaker Lloyd Francis last July, regarding the former administration of the House of Commons. Mr. Francis, in my opinion, did not intend that those comments become public then and, also in my opinion, they would probably have been better left unsaid. However, notwithstanding that, I can tell the House that leaving aside the more spectacular quotes which reached the press, the situation was far worse than outlined. Just as it was inappropriate that the details be divulged last July, nothing would be gained from my reciting them now.
In an earlier political life, I had undertaken a major change of staff and direction in the City of Belleville, in the late 1950s and early 1960s. I had some idea of the problems which could be encountered, and I was part of the Management and Members' Services Committee which requested the then Speaker, Mr. Jerome, undertake an in-depth study of the management of the House of Commons. The decision to ask the Auditor General to do the study was that of the Speaker, but his support came from the Members' Services Committee in 1978.
I am sure that all will recall the seriously confused political situation which existed in Canada during that short period of time. The Progressive Conservative Government, under the leadership of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark), lasted only nine months. During that time, Mr. Speaker Jerome accepted the interim report of the Auditor General. In his comments to the House, he said:
To my knowledge, no Speaker has ever been chosen on the basis of administrative expertise-neither has the Clerk of the House nor the Sergeant-at-Arms with whom the Speaker shares these duties-and yet, we have neither comptroller nor professional administrator within the ranks of the House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker Jerome then undertook to put in place an interim Administrator to begin the clean-up, and he accepted full responsibility for doing so. On behalf of the Government of the day, the late Hon. Walter Baker said:
I say on behalf of the Government that we support the action you have taken with respect to this matter.
That Government was, as I said, short-lived, and Speaker Sauve, in the chair of the thirty-second Parliament, set out to continue the work started by Speaker Jerome. She undertook to change the person of the Administrator who, like his predecessor, faced enormous obstacles. Employees viewed him as an external factor unnecessarily disrupting their lives, and Members quickly sided with employees whom they had known for many years. However, with the full support of the Speaker

November 26, 1985
House of Commons Act
and the Clerk of the day, together with knowledgeable Members of Parliament, the job was undertaken.
Let me now look at some of the results. During that period of time, some 376 administrative positions were eliminated and 94 new ones created. However, during the period, not a single full-time employee of the House was fired or laid off in the effort to reduce costs. Of the 94 new ones, a breakdown should be helpful-personnel, which had been terribly neglected over the years, received 29; the Table Research Branch, 16; computer and electronic services, 27; and miscellaneous, 22, including the Clerk, three, the Administrator, five and the Sergeant-at-Arms, 6. As important, or perhaps more so, is the fact that in the five years from 1980 to 1985, over 500 competitions took place, something that had never happened in the House of Commons previously. As a result of the competitions, 232 employees on staff were promoted and another 241 were promoted or reclassified as a result of ongoing personnel changes.
At the height of the time when questions were being raised about the ethics and the propriety of having an Administrator in the House of Commons, in 1983, the Auditor General undertook a comprehensive follow-up audit of the 1980 report. He said:
The House of Commons now has a comprehensive and well organized financial management operation; excellent briefing materials are provided to members and timely and practical financial reports are given to both Members and House managers. We receive positive feed-back from operating managers on the assistance and support provided by the Comptroller's office.
In short, the staff were even then settling down to enjoy the benefits of good administration, and I think it is fair to say that the majority of Members who pay attention to the administrative system that provides their support services are happy with the results.
Budgets for the operation of the House of Commons during this period when the new Administrator was beginning his duties reflected the expertise of his office. Despite the fact that Members were receiving more and better services than ever before, the annual increase in the budget set aside for the House of Commons was 5 per cent or less. Even though with rampant inflation Government Departments were increasing budgets by 15 per cent to 20 per cent, the House of Commons budget fell below the inflation rate by a large measure.
To outline now all the improved benefits which Members received during this period would take more time than I have at my disposal. Suffice it to say that over 80 per cent of the requests made by the Members' Services Committee were accommodated within the lessened budget. I could also spend more than the time allotted to me discussing and describing the OASIS local area network which has put Members in the position of having the finest electronic support program of any legislature in the world. All of this was accomplished in the period of time I mentioned of lower budgets and clearer administrative services.
While there are always new ideas to be presented for the consideration of the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services and the Board of Internal Economy, either for the administration of the House or for the services offered to Members, the major reforms recommended by the Auditor General in 1980 are now in place. Most in fact have been in place for a number of years and people have adjusted to and now approve of them. Most have no wish to return to the good old days, particularly if they experienced them firsthand. The Chairman of the Special Committee on the Reform of the House of Commons, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), reflected the view of many of his colleagues when he declared the following:
We are now the best paid and supported Parliament in the western world.
To a degree, we have broken new ground in the administration of the House of Commons in Canada, but not entirely. The Province of Ontario has had a similar administrative organization since 1976. Australia has had a similar arrangement since 1954. In New Zealand, a Bill has recently passed establishing the position of general manager to be responsible for administrative services. Two quotes from the Hansard of the New Zealand House during the debate on that Bill might be of interest. I quote the following from New Zealand Hansard:
The rationale behind those changes is to allow the Clerk of the House to concentrate on the smooth running of the House and the important constitutional functions that devolve on the Clerk's office in Parliament. The Clerk's counterpart on the administrative side will exercise a full-time managerial function-thus improving the support services provided to Members of Parliament.
I go on to quote from the New Zealand Hansard:
There is a great deal more administration in this building than there was formerly and I think it is fair to say-without casting any adverse reflections on anyone who has been responsible in the past-that there has been a lack of management services here that needs to be remedied.
Finally, a few years ago the British House had placed before it a recommendation that all the administration be put under the supervision of the Clerk. It is interesting to note that a committee of Members of the British House of Commons rejected that recommendation saying that the plan was simply not workable and would destroy the ability of the Clerk to perform his procedural duties.
In closing, let me say that in the last five years the need to add the position of the Administrator to the Standing Orders and the House of Commons Act has been supported by three Speakers-I cannot, of course, ask the current Speaker to offer an opinion regarding a matter before the House-three Attorneys General, two Clerks and most MPs who have any knowledge of the administration of the House of Commons. This form of administration is either in place or is being carried out in other legislative bodies throughout the western world. The fact of the Administrator in the Canadian House of Commons has existed since 1980. The time has come to include that fact in legislation.

speechtext: That sounds like you.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: I say this as a Member of the House of Commons and as a former employee of the House of Commons. Those Members who are concerned with how Parliament should work should, in my view, all be greatly concerned and should all work to defeat this particular Bill.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Sounds like a Liberal.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The Hon. Member is right. I do sound like a Liberal. I believe that Parliament is supreme. I believe that Parliament should be supreme and that no structure should ever exist to take anything away from the supremacy of Parliament. The Hon. Member across the way would like to say that that is a Liberal principle. I would not have taken that credit myself, but now that he has said it, I will accept it on behalf of myself and hopefully some of my colleagues.
The whole principle of the supremacy of Parliament came to light very recently in a very particular way during discussions on Bill C-45, an Act to grant certain rights and privileges to the employees of this institution. It became quite evident that the majority of Members did not want to give the right to strike to the employees of the House of Commons because it was the view of some that by giving them that right, people outside the Chamber would be able to dictate whether or not Parliament could function. In other words, they argued that it took away from the supremacy of Parliament. I do not happen to think that that was a very legitimate concern at that time because we could designate certain employees as essential and proceed without the rest thus giving them their full rights. However, we are still in the process of debating that particular legislation. It was a concern that was expressed by a great many Members of the House.
I am of the belief that the senior servants of the House should report to the Clerk and that the Clerk should report to the Speaker. With that structure, it is my view that the servants of the House are the employees of the House and not the masters of the House. I believe that it is important for us as legislators to considre that. I will not claim that I am the author of that maxim. However, let me cite Citation No. 13 from Beauchesne's Fifth Edition:
(1)	Within the ambit of its own rules, the House itself may proceed as it chooses; it is a common practice for the House to ignore its own rules by unanimous consent. Thus, bills may be passed through all their stages in one day, or the House may decide to alter its normal order of business or its adjournment hour as it sees fit.
(2)	The House is perfectly able to give consent to set aside its Standing Orders and to give its unanimous consent to waive procedural requirements and precedents concerning notice and things of that sort.
In other words, the House and only the House can be the master of the House of Commons.
Let me continue by quoting from Erskine May. At page 207 it states:
House of Commons Act
The law of Parliament provides the framework for, and determines the nature of, Parliamentary procedure, which consists of the rules and arrangements made by either House for discharging its constitutional functions within that framework.
The principal distinction for practical purposes between parliamentary law and procedure is that any change in the law of Parliament can only be effected by statute, whereas either House is free to modify its own procedure by its independent action; and that for the regulation of procedure recourse is not had to statute except for the purpose of effecting similar procedural changes in both Houses, or of co-ordinating the rules of procedure to changes in the law of Parliament.
In other words, it is an indication that Parliament has to be supreme.
There is another reason for the House not giving consideration to Bill C-252. I fundamentally disagree with the Hon. Member who proposes the Bill who said that it has wide support and has had wide support from Members in the past.

speechtext: I said from knowledgeable Members.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I refer the Hon. Member to the Third Report of the Special Committee on Reform of the House of Commons which the Hon. Member quoted himself. Even if the Hon. Member disagrees with what I have to say today I hope he will consider the opinions which were unanimously adopted by the House in order for the House to function. 1 would like to quote from Chapter VIII of the report under the title Administrative Reform which states:
We believe the legitimate right of members to control the House of Commons should be reinforced. For this reason our First Report proposed a Board of Internal Economy.
Further on, in the same chapter the report states:
Members must not only run the House, they must feel that they are in charge. We place a high priority on restoring the pre-eminence of the House of Commons and of proceedings in the Chamber.
What we glean from the report is that the role of Members in giving direction to the House and how it is to be run should be increased and not decreased.
As I indicated earlier on I think that there should be only one senior officer of the House and that should be the Clerk of the House. I would like to read further from the report in this regard which states:
The role of the Clerk of the House of Commons should be one of leadership and inspiration for all employees of the House. For this reason the Clerk of the House must be, and be seen to be, the principal permanent officer of the House, accountable to it, and its bodies, for operations of the House of Commons.
The committee recommends that the role of the Clerk should be one of leadership. That means first-in charge.
I am sure all Hon. Members have noted by now that, indeed, the committee said something in its report quite different from what we heard earlier today. The special committee also suggested that the role of the Board of Internal Economy be increased. It suggested that the board should be structured having the Speaker, the Deputy Speaker, two members of the Queen's Privy Council, the Leader of the Opposition or his nominee and two other ordinary Members sit on the board. I presume the Hon. Member opposite agrees with this recom-

November 26, 1985
House of Commons Act
mendation since he voted for it when Bill C-63 was adopted on June 27, 1985. There was provision in that Bill for an independent secretariat for the Board of Internal Economy. This would ensure that the Board of Internal Economy would be run as a management team and that its decisions would not be influenced in any way by any forces other than those of the Members of the House of Commons. This is why there was provision for a secretariat. As far as I know, the structure is not yet in place. If we have time this afternoon to debate anything it should be the establishment of just that.
1 am worried about any Bill which wants us to go in the opposite direction to that suggested by the Special Committee on Reform. Notwithstanding the fact that there may well be a need for someone to administer the House, I do not believe we should be structuring anything so as to afford the House and its principal officer three Deputy Ministers. If having a tri-umverate to run a ministry, or any place, was in order then why is it Ministers have only one Deputy Minister and not three? Ministers have much larger departments than that of the Speaker of the House of Commons. It is well known that there should be one Deputy Minister, one person in charge who reports to the elected officials. That is the way all Government departments are structured. Therefore, I believe that strengthening the principle advocated in the Third Report of the Special Committee with respect to the senior person, the person in the role of leadership, being the Clerk of the House reporting to the Speaker of the House should be followed. That structure was recommended and unanimously adopted. It is the proper way for us to go. To move in a diametrically opposite direction at this time for whatever reason is totally unjustified.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I wonder what we have to gain by putting the kind of structure in place proposed by the Hon. Member in his Bill. It certainly is not because a parliamentary committee recommended a similar formula, and it certainly is not because a number of reports have indicated that we are to have three, what I would consider to be assistant deputy ministers, to run the House of Commons.
If the Hon. Member cannot find any better support for his proposal than the references he gave us earlier today, well, Mr. Speaker, I must say I still abide by my initial decision to vote against his proposal and talk out the Bill.

The Hon. Member has indicated to us how some services on Parliament Hill have tremendously improved. Those were the words he used. Some services may have improved. I have two television sets in my office. Like most people I can only watch one at a time. However, there are two there because that is the way the system works. One wonders whether or not some improvements are necessary. I have a machine in my constituency office with a little printer on it which types out press releases if I so desire. Again, I am sure it is very useful although I have never used it.
On the other hand, we have a structure which in my view is very cumbersome. Notwithstanding the fact that we had to improve certain items, we have destroyed many things in our quest for improvement. The Hon. Member opposite says that no employees were fired in the process of improving the House. I am not sure what is meant by "fired" in his terms. But let me say to you, Mr. Speaker, that many employees left not of their own accord. Perhaps people would not call that "firing" necessarily, but some employees who would have preferred to stay, are no longer here. I will put it in those terms.
We have all these gadgets, the so-called improvements, including these excellent briefing materials which the Hon. Member opposite described for us earlier. Yet I asked a messenger in my office to bring a cardboard box to my car so I could bring it to my constituency office, only to be told that because of all these regulations he could only go as far as the door. I had to go outside and get my car from the parking lot and bring it back to the door so he could put the box into the car. I answered very properly that if I had to go outside to get my car, I might just as well bring the box with me and, therefore, I did not need the messenger. The messenger explained to me, and of course I believe him because I know it is true, that this is the way the system works. These are the guidelines with which people in this building have to live. My request did not qualify under a number or kind of delivery.
As much as our system is apparently so improved, and I do not doubt in certain ways it may be better than it was before, let us not believe that everything which has been done in those so-called improvements has been good for the staff or even for Hon. Members of the House of Commons.
To change something means that it is changed, but it does not necessarily mean that it is better. To make the changes advocated in this Bill to amend the House of Commons Act is certainly just one of those examples. It is a change for the purpose of making a change, with plenty of proof that nothing or very little could be better and, in my view, far more could be worse than what it is now.
I ask all Hon. Members to seriously consider the implications of effectively placing another person at a deputy minister level in this House of Commons. I think there should be only one. There are presently two. We should not have three.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have read the legislation introduced by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis). I think there are some matters which have been in dispute over the years in this House of Commons. There have been questions about the administration of the House of Commons and as someone who has sat on the Committee of Management and Members' Services for the last year, I can say that I certainly have had the opportunity to disagree with the administrator just as I have had occasion to disagree with the decisions of the Sergeant-at-Arms and occa-
November 26, 1985

sionally with the Clerks who have decided against me on some occasions in the past. I do not mean to indicate that that is a particular reason for being either in favour of or against this particular legislation.
I do not want to see us with three Deputy Ministers, but I do not think that is the main point behind this particular legislation. My particular reason for liking the legislation before us and for wanting us to view it in more depth in a legislative committee-which is what would happen if the Government were in a position to allow this to go to committee-is that 1 think it recognizes the de facto situation in the House of Commons at the present time.
All three Parties on the Committee of Management and Members' Services expect the Sergeant-at-Arms, the Administrator and, on occasion, the Clerk to come before it. Member of the Liberal Party brought up in his speech are under the direct responsibility of the Administrator at the present time. Member happens to need a computer in his office as opposed to someone who comes from a riding which is, in my case, 2,000 miles away. Instead, we should be looking at how we want the House to be administered and what controls we want over the House. We should also be looking at what is the exact role of the Board of Internal Economy. That is something which can be considered in dealing with this legislation in committee. That is one of the reasons I would like to see this legislation go forward.
I will not be speaking very long on the legislation as it is specifically before us. I do want to say something in reaction to the Hon. Member who introduced the legislation. I must say that there were parts of his speech with which I was in disagreement. There are still a number of problems in the House of Commons.
House of Commons Act
Another piece of legislation with which we are dealing at this time is Bill C-45, regarding the collective bargaining rights of people who work on the Hill. Many Hon. Members who are presently in the House were involved in debate on this Bill and it has been brought out that there are a number of problems which still exist. There are a number of problems dealing with classification, staffing levels and hiring procedures. Those problems still exist. But that is not the particular subject of this legislation. subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on Bill C-252 introduced by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis). First let me say that I will not be supporting the Bill in principle. I would like to point out, however, that I do not feel it is a bad Bill. The only thing I question is the timing of it.
I would like to speak today about basically three points; the effects which the McGrath Committee Report on Parliamentary Reform will have on this particular House and how we should be looking at that as Parliamentarians after the great amount of effort and dedication was put into this report. I would also like to speak about the Board of Internal Economy, of which I have been privileged to become one of the commissioners. I would also like to discuss Bill C-63.
Bill C-252, as presented to the House by the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings, recommends that we bring about change. There is nothing wrong with change, but change for the sake of change becomes very dangerous when dealing with this institution. I do not believe that he brought this Bill in merely for the sake of change. I am sure he brought it in to bring about improvements in the administration of this House. I want to focus on the improved conditions that we on Parliament Hill have provided for the staff, who are of prime importance for MPs and to the ultimate benefit of the taxpayer, the people we serve.
I agree with the Hon. Member that we must maintain a high standard of integrity. We also must maintain a high standard of performance. That can only be attained by having the tools to work with. On June 27, 1985, this Government presented Bill C-63 to this House. That Bill did not make the changes recommended here today. I do not know why it was not discussed at that time. However, Bill C-63 is excellent legislation. It gave us a new Board of Internal Economy which encompasses all Parties in the House and allows private Members to participate in the decision-making process regarding Parliament Hill. Prior to this, the Board was composed of the Speaker and two Members, generally Privy Counsellors. With the inception of the Board-

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Four Members.

November 26, 1985
House of Commons Act

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I am informed that there were four Members on the Board previously. However, private Members were not represented. Since the inception of certain recommendations from the McGrath Report every Member in this House has a voice on this issue. It also gave Members the opportunity to raise questions concerning the management of the House through a designated member of the Board. That is a great improvement. It allows Members to participate in the day-to-day operations of Parliament Hill.
The Board was also to establish a secretariat. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) made mention of the fact that we had not as yet named a secretariat. I want to point out that we are working in that direction but we have not as yet met often enough to resolve the question of the direction in which we should be going with the administration or financial management of this institution. We have met on merely three occasions. However, I can assure all Members that a secretariat will be chosen and it will be answerable to Members in this House. We as a Board of Internal Economy will provide the guidance required for our staff, whether they be administrative or anything else, because ultimately they answer to us.
This House commissioned the McGrath committee report concerning parliamentary reform. As I pointed out, they covered numerous aspects of the operations of Parliament Hill as well as procedures in the House. I honestly believe that we must give this report full consideration before we enter into further legislative or administrative changes. As the Right Hon. Prime Minister has said on so many occasions, it is a tremendous report in all aspects. It not only makes numerous excellent recommendations but, more importantly, it represents all Members of the House.
I honestly believe as well that were we to allow this Bill to proceed we would virtually usurp the power of the new Board of Internal Economy established by this House. I am not saying that it will not happen that the Board may deem it suitable to make certain recommendations in line with what the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings has put forward, but I would not want to be too hasty in going in that particular direction.
The Board is in its infancy. We are discussing numerous aspects of change which would improve the plight of a number of groups in this operation. Having been a Member and president of a trade union, I feel it is important that each Member of our staff be given full consideration and as many rights as humanly possible, while at the same time maintaining the high standards which have always existed in Parliament.
The new legislative committees we have established are, as well, something which the Board is studying. Here again we have something in its infancy, something very new to Parliament, and this, along with other innovations, should be dealt with in an orderly fashion, one by one. I know that the administration aspect will be dealt with as fairly and judiciously as possible.
There are other Members who wish to speak on this subject. Without a doubt, I, as a Commissioner of the Board of Internal Economy and Member of Parliament, feel that we cannot stand still. We must continue to try to focus our attention on improving conditions for Members of Parliament and for all of those who work on Parliament Hill. The eventual outcome will be a benefit to all Canadians, not only to those of us here, but to those whom we serve.
I would like to conclude my remarks by asking the House to consider delaying, for a short period of time, its decision on this very important matter and to allow those of us who have been designated to consider improvement to the financial and administrative aspects of the House, and to look at the entire program we must deal with on the Hill, prior to coming forward with changed legislation of this nature.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have looked with great care at Bill C-252 in the name of the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis), who is Vice-Chairman of the Management and Members' Services Committee. I must say that on the surface the Bill appears to be quite inoffensive, even innocuous. All it is asking is that the administrator be allowed to prepare, table, and defend his own estimates. However, there is a subtlety in this Bill which has been alluded to by my hon. friend for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), and by my hon. friend on the Government side who has just spoken. The subtlety is that the Bill is creating a new officer of the House, a third officer of the House in addition to the two who have traditionally been in charge; namely, the Clerk of the House and the Sergeant-at-Arms.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: It's about time.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The Chairman of the Management and Members' Services Committee is here and has kindly allowed me to use up the remaining time. He indicated to me that if he were speaking on this Bill he would probably be in favour of it, but with reservations. I suppose that is not a bad position to be in. I would put my emphasis, Your Honour, on the reservations. To agree to a piece of legislation which creates a third officer of the House with equal rank to the Clerk of the House, that officer being the administrator, runs directly counter to a truly splendid and outstanding report, the McGrath committee report which I think is going to be a hallmark of reform for many generations of parliamentarians.
Recommendation 8.2 of this report reads:
We recommend that the Clerk of the House of Commons have ultimate responsibility for the administration of the House.
Having been an alternate member of that reform committee and having enjoyed my association with the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and with the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings, I certainly stand by that recommendation.
The report notes that the Clerk of the House has concentrated more and more of his time on procedural matters. It goes on
November 26, 1985

to say that we understand the need for such expertise in the Elouse but that the role of the Clerk of the House of Commons must be one of leadership and inspiration for all employees of the House. For this reason, the report says that he must be seen as the principal and permanent officer of the House.
The role of the Clerk of the House of Commons has traditionally been that of the chief permanent officer. It is said, for example, that he is learned and highly specialized. He is an expert in legislative procedure but, traditionally, he has wide experience in parliamentary administration.
Mir. Ellis: He had absolutely none, you dunderhead.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
If the Hon. Member will relax for a moment before he gets his dander too high, he will appreciate what they have done in Great Britain to deal with this matter. In Great Britain they have recongized as well that the Clerk of the House has more and more responsibilities for procedural matters. They have not, therefore, decided to create a third permanent officer or, as my hon. friend for Glengarry-Pre-scott-Russell indicated, another deputy minister. In the British House of Commons they have created a department of administration. The department of administration is headed by a clerk administrator who is directly responsible to the Clerk of the House. He is the man who looks after all of the administrative details, but he is not an independent, separate figure running an administrative department apart from the authority of the Clerk himself.
I suppose some Hon. Members would argue that we ought to have a third permanent position, another officer in the House of Commons. We have the Clerk and the Segeant-at-Arms, so why do we not have a third?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Yes, why?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The Sergeant-at-Arms has, of course, a long and traditional role in the House of Commons extending back a very, very long way, to the time of King Richard II of England who decided that the Speaker needed someone to protect him. The Sergeant-at-Arms originally was a body guard to the Speaker. Later when that responsibility was no longer required, his functions became those of one who looked after the precincts of the House and ensured that there were good housekeeping procedures and proper security in place. That is a long-standing traditional post.
No one is arguing against good administration. I think the Hon. Member for Prince Edward-Hastings jumped to the conclusion that in opposing his Bill we are against good administration of the House of Commons. Of course we are not. We want effective, efficient and cost effective administration. No one is arguing that at all.
However, the big danger which lurks in the Hon. Member's legislation is that, more and more, the House of Commons is going to become just another department of government. It can never be that. The purpose of Parliament is to be the watchdog over the Government of Canada and we need our allies. Our allies are the Auditor General, the Clerk at the
Adjournment Debate
table, the Sergeant-at-Arms and all of those attributes which make our watchdog role as efficient as it can possibly be.
The danger in Bill C-252 is that it sets up a separate administrative structure quite apart from the House of Commons, operating at arm's length. As a result, the teamwork which ought to exist with the Speaker, the Clerk, the Sergeant-at-Arms and the subsidiary figure who is responsible for administration, can be broken down. The McGrath committee report drew attention to that danger. No less a person than the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), who was the vicechairman of the reform committee, indicated at one of those meetings that his feeling was that parliamentarians would be better served if there were a number of people who were not necessarily competing against one another to serve parliamentarians, but complementing one another.
I think the great fear among parliamentarians about a separate administrative arrangement is that it will increasingly become the tail that wags the dog. It will become the force that directs the work of parliamentarians.
My hon. friend, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell was quite correct in drawing attention to the fact that the House of Commons must be in the charge of the Members themselves, and we cannot set up a separate administrative unit that begins to direct and control them. The McGrath Committee Report drew clear attention to that. If time permits me, at page 50 it said-[DOT]
