subtopic: CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-TREATMENT OF VISITORS AT EDMONTON INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-TREATMENT OF VISITORS AT EDMONTON INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 30 I put a question to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. MacKay) relating to some treatment that has been extended to incoming passengers at the Edmonton International Airport by the Customs and Immigration officials. At that time the Minister indicated to me that he would look into the matter to

November 26, 1985
Adjournment Debate
see if there was a way to improve upon the treatment extended not only to Canadians but to other tourists as well.
At the outset, let me indicate to you that I do not intend to take my entire time to make a presentation. It is my hope that we will hear from the Parliamentary Secretary about how we can improve the situation at the airport.
I have several reasons for raising this concern. I have had representations from my constituents with regard to treatment that has been afforded to them. Individuals on the Council of the City of Edmonton have raised this concern. Furthermore, provincial Ministers of the Crown from the Province of Alberta have shared a similar concern about the poor treatment extended not only to Canadians but to visitors to Canada.
I acknowledge the difficulty that these officials have in performing their tasks, but it is essential that these officers convey a positive and good attitude to fellow Canadians and convey a warm atmosphere to tourists who come here on a regular basis. The tourism industry is very important not only to our country, but to our province and our city. I know that the Minister of National Revenue and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) have looked into this matter. I hope that the response we will receive will indicate that the situation will improve.
In fairness to the Customs officials, let me indicate that once this issue received some media attention I received calls from individuals who have been very impressed by the courteous manner in which they have been treated. Obviously there are two sides to this issue. I only want to stress that it is essential that we as Canadians always extend a warm hand of friendship to whomever visits our country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Valcourt (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CUSTOMS AND EXCISE-TREATMENT OF VISITORS AT EDMONTON INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to respond to the Hon. Member's concerns regarding the treatment of tourists and visitors to Canada by Customs officers at the Edmonton International Airport. I can advise the Hon. Member that the Department of National Revenue shares his concern about the importance of tourism to the Canadian economy and that the role which Customs officers play in welcoming visitors to Canada is indeed important.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister has been aware of the situation for some time, and assures us that this kind of treatment vis-avis travellers will not be tolerated, not in Edmonton and not at any other point of entry in this country.
Last June, senior officials from the Department were sent to examine the situation at the Edmonton International Airport.
After their visit, a series of measures were put in place. These measures deal with the training of officers in the kind of attitude and behaviour expected of them, their regulations and interaction with travellersand especially the public's perception of the role of a customs officer. In addition, a number of measures are being considered, and some have already been
implemented, to make customs officers adopt a more positive and sensitive attitude, covering areas such as multiculturalism, conflict resolution, neutralizing delicate situations, interview techniques, interprovincial communications on the job, and so on.
A three-day experiment will be held in Edmonton in November, to analyze the kind of problems encountered at high risk and high volume offices. Customs officers have now received more training in connection with their responsibilities under the Immigration Act. Furthermore, useful discussions have been held with provincial representatives, and recommendations for simplifying certain customs procedures have been submitted to them. We are now awaiting their reply.
Officials are continuing to monitor customs activities closely at the Edmonton airport. The Minister is confident that the action taken by his officials at Edmonton will ensure that a courteous and professional welcome is extended to all persons entering Canada, which Canadians have come to expect of the Customs service.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the 1985 Auditor General's Report supports the fact that Customs and Excise is working toward providing a more efficient and courteous service to the public.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-EXTRADITION OF UNITED STATES CITIZENS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-EXTRADITION OF UNITED STATES CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will recall that on November 7, 1985 during Question Period 1 asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) about the cases of Charles Ng and Joseph Kindler, two Americans who are currently being held in custody in Canada.
You will recall that in the case of Charles Ng, he was apprehended in one of our western cities and charged with armed robbery as well as with attempted murder. Then it came to light that he was the subject of a search across North America, and perhaps world-wide. He was wanted for questioning in connection with some mass murders in the state of California.
You will recall, Sir, that there were some particularly grizzly murders in the state of California and Charles Ng, although he had not been charged with these offences, was wanted for questioning in connection with them.
That raised great concerns on the part of my constituents, and 1 know on the part of all Canadians. I had letters, telephone calls and personal inquiries in large numbers from people who were most concerned that an American citizen who allegedly had committed extremely serious crimes in the United States for which there was capital punishment should be here in Canada; we should be shipping him back to the United States as quickly as possible.
November 26, 1985

Those fears were compounded because shortly after that another case came to light, that of Joseph Kindler. This man had been convicted in the United States of capital offences, had escaped custody and had come to Canada. That, on top of the Charles Ng case, really got Canadian people extremely upset and excited about what was going on in this country.
On the surface, those cases have some similarity. There was the whole matter of extradition of people who had allegedly committed crimes in the United States and were now in custody in Canada. However, there were in fact some differences between the two cases.
In the case of Charles Ng, as I indicated, at the time he was apprehended in this country he had not been charged with any offences in the United States. At that time the Americans had not made any request for extradition. Since then, of course, a number of charges have been laid in the State of California against Charles Ng. In fact, I think there are between eight to ten separate charges of murder outstanding, as well as other charges, in connection with the case.
To the best of my knowledge, and on November 7 the Minister indicated in response to my question that at that time the State of California and the United States had not made a formal request for the extradition of Charles Ng. I am hoping tonight, for one thing, that we can learn from the Parliamentary Secretary what is the state of affairs now and whether there has been a request for extradition of Charles Ng. We realize that there can be no extradition until there is a request.
In the case of Joseph Kindler, however, it was very different. There had been a request for extradition. Joseph Kindler had made an application to the courts in this country to stave off that request. As I understand it, his application was based strictly upon the point that he would be facing capital punishment in the United States, that he was not facing capital punishment here and that it would be unfair, improper and unjust under our Charter of Rights for us to send him back to the United States where he would be facing a death penalty sentence. That case, as I understand it again from the Minister, has been proceeded on and now is awaiting written argument from Mr. Kindler's lawyer being presented to the Minister, all the court proceedings having been dismissed. Then the Minister indicated that probably there would be an oral hearing in front of him as well, and that it would be after that that he would be making a decision as to what to do in the case of Mr. Kindler.
Both those cases are of extremely serious concern to Canadians. They are concerned, first of all, because there is a feeling that it is unfair and improper that someone should be able to come up here and get away from American justice just because he or she faces a death penalty in the United States and does not face one here. Of course there is also a broader concern that Canada could very well become a haven for fugitives from American justice or for fugitives from foreign justice around the world. If we look at some of the acts of terrorism in various countries around the world where people
Adjournment Debate
face the death penalty, theoretically, if Mr. Ng and Mr. Kindler were allowed to escape the situation and use Canada as a shelter, we could very well become the repository for all sorts of international terrorists and fugitives from every corner and cranny of the world.
Those are the basic concerns of Canadians. I think it broadens into their general concern about the issue of capital punishment. We have had expressions of extreme concern for many years about the reinstatement of capital punishment in Canada. It seems to me that the cases of Charles Ng and Joseph Kindler highlight that concern very sharply.
I hope we hear from the Parliamentary Secretary tonight an update of the situation of Charles Ng. Hopefully we will send him back to the United States to face justice there just as quickly as possible. Also I hope we will hear an update on the case of Joseph Kindler. Hopefully we will send him back to the United States for his Christmas dinner. I do not think any Canadian wants to see him around any longer than he has to be.
I would also like to hear from the Parliamentary Secretary about just where we stand on the entire question of a free debate on capital punishment. That is really the key and underlying issue in all of these cases. I am looking forward to the comments of the Parliamentary Secretary regarding all of these items.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Valcourt (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-EXTRADITION OF UNITED STATES CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for the concern he has expressed. I certainly agree that many Canadian citizens are also concerned about the points which he has made here today.
The Hon. Member properly pointed out that he brought up the question on November 17. It was again raised on November 19 by the Hon. Member for Calgary East (Mr. Kindy). At that time, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) advised the House that in the case of Charles Ng, no request had yet been received from the United States for his extradition. That situation has not changed as of yet. No procedure has been begun asking for extradition.
In the case of Joseph Kindler, as the Minister pointed out to the Hon. Member for Calgary East on November 19, the only change in that situation has been the extension given to the solicitors of Mr. Ng to prepare their submission to the Minister. The Hon. Member will recall that the Minister stated that the position of that individual was that his extradition to the United States should be asserted with conditions. In order to properly prepare their case and make it to the Minister, his solicitors needed further time.
I am certain that although Canadians may be very concerned about criminals from other countries being in Canada, they are not so concerned that they will deprive these individuals of the right to be heard. I believe the Minister has to be commended for this, and we understand that this is what guided him in the granting of this extension.

November 26, 1985
Adjournment Debate
As the Hon. Member will certainly understand, I cannot give him the assurance that Mr. Kindler will be returned home for Christmas. However, it is my understanding that the Minister will not unduly delay any decision in that case. As for the other case, there is no change of status.
The Hon. Member also requested that I address the question of when we will have a debate in this House on the issue of capital punishment. subtopic: VISIBLE MINORITIES-JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II
VISIBLE MINORITIES-JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate having this opportunity to say a little more about a question I asked many months ago. On May 23, I asked the then Minister of State for Multiculturalism about the Government's plans regarding redress for Japanese Canadians and specifically redress for the great injustice which was done them in the 1940s when they were dispossessed, resettled in the interior and faced, even after the Second World War had ended, the discriminatory actions of the Canadian Government.
At the time I specifically asked the Minister if he actually believes that the Opposition's failure to agree to an imposed settlement prevented him from negotiating with the National Association of Japanese-Canadians. That question elicited the following key statement from the Minister:
Mr. Speaker, we never refer to anything we are doing in terms of our conversations as negotiations with the Japanese-Canadians.
He added some observations to that which I need not get into.
I have waited patiently on this matter because I wanted to give the Government the opportunity to resolve the matter. As well, I was aware that the National Association of Japanese Canadians was involved in its own program to demonstrate the extent of losses that were suffered. Even at this point I may say that the association is still involved in a program which, over the next few months, will provide an unprecedented description, an accounting, of the losses which Japanese Canadians suffered in a material way. By that means the incredible psychic and social costs which were inflicted upon them at the time will be underscored.
It seems to me appropriate this evening to investigate this matter a little further and place some principles on the record. We have a new Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Jelinek). He has had some three months in office. In the last couple of weeks there have been some very disturbing indications of the position which the Government may come to with respect to this matter, particularly indications which were provided in a press release from the City of Ottawa on November 17, following the meeting of the Canadian Multiculturalism Council which is advisory to the Minister. The
council suggested that the redress policy should include among its points a settlement which is symbolic in terms of monetary award, and that it should be directed more toward the prevention of future wrongs upon any ethnocultural groups rather than a correction of past injustices. It went on to suggest that the establishment of a multicultural foundation with a mandate to foster understanding and friendship among ethnocultural communities might be such an expression.
That statement raised the gravest concerns in my mind about the Government's will to move on the indications which it gave, first of all as the opposition Party in June of 1984, and then from the Minister's office in December of 1984. After all, it was the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who questioned Mr. Trudeau, the then Prime Minister, about this matter. It was he who aroused hopes for the first time in decades that if he became Prime Minister he would have the will to do something about it.
On December 15 the Multiculturalism Directorate suggested in a release that there had been agreement between the Minister and the National Association of Japanese Canadians to negotiate something. Sadly enough that promise of December 15, 1984 was turned into an attempt at an imposed settlement before January had ended. It included a refusal to negotiate with the National Association of Japanese Canadians.
Part of my unhappiness about this matter-I might even say my umbrage at what has developed-is the fact that the Prime Minister has been capable of maligning the Opposition by his description of those events. Upon assuming office he said in a letter to a private citizen:
-my Government took the initiative in addressing the concerns of the Japanese-Canadian community that the injustices inflicted-
He states further:
After extensive consultation with the community, the matter was brought before Parliament on January 28 in the form of an all-Party resolution. As you may know, we were disappointed in our hope that the opposition parties would forgo partisan considerations and demonstrate the resolution's wide support among Canadians by giving unanimous consent to its passage.
That sentence is most interestingly worded. How could our consent here to an all-Party resolution indicate wide-spread support for it? Surely a redress proposal needs to have the support of the Japanese Canadian community. That was exactly what the Government had refused to do earlier in January of 1985.
It is then in this context of refusal to negotiate and the rejection of compensation for individuals that we stand. It is in this context that I want to say categorically that it seems to me inconceivable that we could have the arbitrary and dictatorial actions of Government in the 1940s during and after the Second World War redressed by the arbitrary action of a Government in 1985 or 1986. It seems to me absolutely imperative that if there is to be a proper settlement it will have to be negotiated with the National Association of Japanese Canadians.
It seems to me imperative, then, that there be substantial discussions on the details of redress settlement. It is imperative



November 26, 1985

that a parliamentary statement which will have the support of all Parties be developed in just such negotiations with the National Association of Japanese Canadians. It is imperative that this recognize the unjust actions of the Government of Canada in the 1940s. There has to be an agreement, too on the substance of redress. It is conceivable that that might find an institutional form. But I do not think we should rule out the possibility that individuals deserve compensation.
On a concluding note, it seems to me imperative that this same redress settlement include recognition that there were abuses flowing not just from the War Measures Act but in the area of citizenship and in the area of the exclusion of persons from British Columbia well after the war. A redress agreement has to include recognition of all of these elements and cannot be satisfactory to the Canadian people any more than to the National Association of Japanese Canadians unless it includes these.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Multiculturalism); Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subtopic: VISIBLE MINORITIES-JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Let me just begin my response to the Hon. Member by saying that he should be applauding, and, indeed, every Hon. Member of the Opposition should be applauding this Government's initiative, because for 42 or 43 years no national Government took the initiative to begin discussions, acknowledging that a bad problem, an unforgettable problem, took place some 42 or 43 years before. In fact, the commitment made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was Leader of the Opposition, and since becoming Prime Minister, is a commitment which we are following, namely, that this Government will acknowledge these wrongs for the first time in 43 years. There will be a form of apology and there is going to be a fair redress package. In fact, some measures, such as the War Measures Act, are already being amended in such a way as to satisfy those people who were hurt by those actions in the early 1940s.
No other Government took that initiative. In fact, the previous administration under Prime Minister Trudeau very clearly said that Government should not get involved in a
Adjournment Debate
redress package, and that the Liberal Government would not get so involved in any way, shape or form.
What I have begun to do in my three months as Minister responsible for multiculturalism is to bring within the scope of discussions across the country not only the National Association of Japanese Canadians but all other interested parties, including the Japanese Canadian Redress Association of Survivors, which is an interested group of survivors from those years, and the Canadian Multicultural Council. 1 would think the Hon. Member should find the statement from the CMC a very positive one and one which is making an input toward my deliberations. My provincial counterparts and all other interested parties across the country are included in the discussions.
I have continually had discussions with them in the past three months building on the foundation which my predecessor had achieved in the previous year. I believe that this is not simply a Japanese Canadian problem. This is a Canadian problem. We must try to get as much input from as broad a section of Canadians as possible.
When I have finally compiled this type of input which 1 require to make a recommendation, then I will do so to Cabinet. It will include an acknowledgement, as the Prime Minister has promised, and an apology of some form, and it will include a fair redress package, fair to the Canadian public and to Canada as a whole.
The main purpose of this is to make sure that this type of atrocity which happened 42 or 43 years ago will never happen in this country again. I take pride in the fact that the Prime Minister took the initiative on behalf of the Government of Canada, for the first time in 42 or 43 years, to deal with this matter. I look forward to having input from as broad a range of Canadians as possible so that we can develop the fairest possible package for Canadians as a whole.
